units.translation: This word means a wild boar in Homer, a locust in Aeschylus, whose verse the scholiast of the Venetian B manuscript of Homer's Iliad 9, 539 preserved. In a scholium written by a third hand: χλούνην [the wild boar] some say means foaming; for χλουδεῖν [to foam] some Dorians used to say; others say it means a rogue; for one of the ancient iambic poets said: “ἀνὴρ ὅδ᾽ ἐσπέρης καθεύδοντα | ἄπουν ἔδησε χλούνην” [this man in the evening bound a footless wild boar sleeping] (χλούνην ἀπ᾿ ὧν ἔδυσε Meineke on Hipponax's fragment p. 121.) And Xenophon (the name is corrupt) said that χλούνην is a kind of Indian (should be written a kind of locust), just as in Aeschylus in the Edonians (fr. 63) “μακροσκελὴς μὲν ἄρα ρα μὴ χλούνης (thus the codex, not ἄρα μαχλούνης as Villoison) τις ἢ (ἢ with iota subscript Villoison, ἦν Hermann).” Eustathius p. 772, 53. That χλούνης also means a castrated animal, not only Aeschylus provides usage, but also Aelian especially in his work On Providence, calling χλούνην the castrated one; and Aristotle according to the geographer calls χλούνην σῦν the castrated boar. "He says that this interpretation was utterly rejected by Aristophanes the grammarian. See Nauck, Aristoph. Byz. fragm. p. 118. 120. In Opusc. 5. p. 13. I said that Aeschylus perhaps wrote ΑΓΓ. μακροσκελὴς μέν. ΛΥΚ. ἆρα μὴ χλούνης τις ἦν; so that χλούνης would mean a locust. For on Theocritus' verse 10, 18 “μάντις τοι τὰν νύκτα χροΐζεται ὁ καλαμαία,” [the locust, the seer, will touch your skin at night] the scholiast noted this: ἴσως οὖν ὁ Θεόκριτος τὴν ἰσχνὴν εἰπεῖν θέλων καὶ διεφθινηκυίαν τοῦτό φησιν. ἢ τὴν ἐπιβλαβές καὶ χαλεπὸν ὁρῶσαν. Ἀρίσταρχος γὰρ ἐν ὑπομνήματι Λυκούργου Αἰσχύλου τὴν ἀκρίδα φησὶ ταύτην, εἰ προσβλέψει τινὶ τῶν ζώων, ἐκείνῳ κακὸν γίνεσθαι. ἔστι δὲ χλωρὰ καὶ περιμήκεις τοὺς πόδας ἔχουσα καὶ λεπτοὺς, καὶ συνεχῶς αὐτοὺς κινοῦσα. [Perhaps Theocritus, wishing to say that she is thin and wasted, says this. Or that she looks harmful and dangerous. For Aristarchus in his commentary on the Lycurgus of Aeschylus says that this locust, if it looks at any animal, brings harm to it. It is green and has very long, thin legs, and moves them constantly.] and after a few words, that very word μακροσκελής [long-legged], but wrongly written μακρόσκελος, is said of that little creature: ἢ ή σὴ ἐρωμένη η ἐοικυῖα τῇ καλαμαίᾳ ὀνομαζομένη, τῇ πρὸς μαντείας ἐπιτηδείᾳ, περιβαλεῖται τὸν χρῶτά σου κατὰ τὴν νύκτα · τουτέστιν, ἡ ἰσχνὴ καὶ λεπτὴ καὶ μακροσκελής συγκοιμηθήσεταί σοι. [Or your beloved, resembling the so-called locust, which is suitable for divination, will embrace your skin at night; that is, the thin, slender, long-legged one will sleep with you.] That commentary of Aristarchus on the Lycurgus embraced the whole tetralogy, and it could not have been confined to the Lycurgus alone, but some of the things read in the preceding tragedies could also have been explained. Therefore I suspected that what Aristarchus discussed pertains to that very verse of the Edonians, and in the things which the Homeric scholiast cites from some book of Xenophon (perhaps from the Silloi of Xenophanes), it should be written γένος τι ἀκρίδων [a kind of locust]." HERMANN. p. 326.
